title: Long Division Grade 5: 2-Digit Divisors Made Simple (DMSB) + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master long division grade 5 with the DMSB cycle: divide by 2-digit divisors, estimate each digit, handle remainders. Free 8-question quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: Grade 5 is where dividing by a single digit turns into dividing by numbers like 24 and 37. Here is the DMSB cycle that makes 2-digit divisors manageable, plus a quick quiz to test it.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 4 child the sum 96 ÷ 4 and most will get there. Hand a Grade 5 child 736 ÷ 23 and something changes — the divisor no longer fits into your times tables, and the guessing begins. That jump, from a one-digit divisor to a two-digit one, is the whole story of long division grade 5. The mechanics are identical to what children already know; what is new is that every step now needs an estimate before it needs an answer.

I have taught this to plenty of ten-year-olds, and the ones who struggle almost never struggle with the division itself. They struggle because nobody showed them the rhythm. Long division is not one operation — it is the same four small moves repeated until the number runs out. Get the rhythm and 2-digit divisors stop being scary.

The DMSB cycle: the heartbeat of long division grade 5

DMSB stands for Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down. You do those four things, in that order, then loop back to Divide and do them again with the next digit. That is it. NCERT calls it the long division algorithm; children remember it as DMSB because the four letters give them something to hold on to when they lose their place.

StepWhat you doExample: 736 ÷ 23
DivideHow many times does the divisor fit the current number?73 ÷ 23 ≈ 3
MultiplyMultiply that digit by the divisor3 × 23 = 69
SubtractTake it away to find what is left73 − 69 = 4
Bring downPull the next digit down beside the remainderbring down 6 → 46

After the bring-down you have 46, so you loop: 46 ÷ 23 = 2, then 2 × 23 = 46, then 46 − 46 = 0. Nothing left to bring down, so you stop. The quotient is 32 with remainder 0. Four moves, twice through, done.

Estimating each quotient digit — the real Grade 5 skill

Here is the part that trips children up, and the part worksheets rarely explain. When the divisor is 23, you cannot instantly recall how many 23s are in 73. So you round. Think of 23 as roughly 20, and ask how many 20s fit into 73 — about 3. Test it: 3 × 23 = 69, which fits under 73. Good.

The estimate is a starting guess, not a verdict. Two things can go wrong, and both are easy to fix:

  • Guess too big: if 3 × 23 had come to more than 73, the digit is too large — drop to 2 and try again.
  • Guess too small: after subtracting, if what is left is bigger than the divisor, the digit was too small — nudge it up by one.

I tell students to round the divisor to the nearest ten and the two-digit division becomes a one-digit division they already know. Divisor 37? Think 40. Divisor 24? Think 20. It is an educated guess, and being allowed to guess-and-check is oddly freeing for a child who thought maths was about knowing instantly.

Rounding down vs rounding up

One honest caveat: rounding 37 down to 40 makes your first guess a touch small, so you may need to bump the digit up. Rounding 24 up to 20 makes your guess a touch big, so you may need to drop it. That is not a mistake — it is the check doing its job. Nobody nails every quotient digit first time, and pretending otherwise sets children up to feel stupid when they do exactly what expert dividers do.

What to do with the remainder

Not every division ends in a clean zero. Take 500 ÷ 16. The algorithm gives 31, and after the last subtraction you are left with 4. Since 4 is smaller than 16, you cannot divide again — that 4 is the remainder. We write it as 31 remainder 4, or in NCERT terms, quotient 31 and remainder 4.

A remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. If yours is bigger or equal, you stopped one step too early — the last quotient digit needed to be one larger. This single rule catches more errors than any other, so it is worth saying out loud every single time.

Always check: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend

This is the step children skip and parents should insist on. To confirm 500 ÷ 16 = 31 remainder 4, multiply the divisor by the quotient and add the remainder back: 16 × 31 = 496, and 496 + 4 = 500. That matches the number we started with, so the answer is right.

The beauty of this check is that it turns division into a multiplication you can verify independently. If the total does not come back to the dividend, something slipped — usually a subtraction error or a quotient digit off by one. In my experience, a child who checks every answer this way stops making careless mistakes within a fortnight, because the check itself teaches them where they tend to go wrong.

A sensible practice order

Do not throw messy four-digit sums at a child on day one. Build up. Start with divisors that are exact multiples of ten (like 20 or 30) so the estimating is trivial. Then move to friendly divisors near a ten (21, 19, 31). Only then tackle the awkward ones in the middle like 24 or 37, and finally sums that leave remainders. Ten minutes a day on this ladder beats an hour of frustration on a random worksheet.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly what we covered — the DMSB cycle, estimating quotient digits, remainders, and the check. Let your child work each one on paper first, then read the explanation. When they are ready for graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives dozens of 2-digit-divisor problems with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 5 Long Division Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on 2-digit divisors, the DMSB cycle, estimating and remainders. Work each on paper, then press Check my score.

questions.q: What do the letters DMSB stand for?
questions.explanation: DMSB is Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down — the four steps you repeat in long division.

questions.q: To estimate 73 ÷ 23, which rounding helps most?
questions.explanation: Round the divisor 23 down to 20. About 3 twenties fit into 73, so 3 is a good first guess.
73 ÷ 23 = 3 (3 × 23 = 69, remainder 4); bring down 6 to get 46; 46 ÷ 23 = 2. Quotient 32, remainder 0.

questions.q: After subtracting, the number left is BIGGER than the divisor. What went wrong?
options: The quotient digit was too small
The quotient digit was too big
You forgot to bring a digit down
questions.explanation: A leftover bigger than the divisor means the divisor still fits again, so the quotient digit needs to go up by one.
16 fits into 500 thirty-one times: 16 × 31 = 496, and 500 − 496 = 4. So 31 remainder 4.
If the remainder is equal to or bigger than the divisor, you could divide once more, so it must be smaller.

questions.q: Which check confirms a long division answer?
questions.explanation: Multiply divisor by quotient and add the remainder; it should equal the dividend you started with.

questions.q: You solved 852 ÷ 12 = 71. Which check proves it is correct?
questions.explanation: With remainder 0, divisor × quotient should equal the dividend: 12 × 71 = 852. It matches, so the answer is right.

faq.q: What is new about long division in Grade 5?
faq.a: Grade 4 divides by a single digit; Grade 5 extends this to 2-digit divisors like 23 or 37. The DMSB steps are identical — the new skill is estimating each quotient digit because the divisor no longer sits in the times tables.

faq.q: How do you estimate a quotient digit with a 2-digit divisor?
faq.a: Round the divisor to the nearest ten, then divide by that. For 73 ÷ 23, treat 23 as 20 and ask how many 20s fit 73 — about 3. Test it with a multiplication and adjust up or down if needed.

faq.q: What should I do with the remainder?
faq.a: The remainder is what is left when the divisor no longer fits. It must be smaller than the divisor; if it is not, the last quotient digit was too small. Write the answer as, for example, 31 remainder 4.

faq.q: How can my child check a long division answer?
faq.a: Use divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend. For 500 ÷ 16 = 31 remainder 4, check 16 × 31 + 4 = 500. If it does not come back to the starting number, there is a mistake to hunt down.
